blocks.text: LangChain agents can already call tools, but for a long time every tool meant someone hand wrote a wrapper class for it.
The langchain-mcp-adapters package removes that requirement by letting an agent pull tools straight from any MCP server.
This lesson covers how the adapter works, how to wire it into an agent executor, and why that saves so much integration work.
1. Why LangChain Needs MCP

blocks.alt: A LangChain agent reaches through the MCP adapter into an MCP server

blocks.text: LangChain became popular because it let developers compose prompts, models, and tools into working agents quickly.
The catch was that every single tool, a search API, a database reader, a file system helper, needed its own hand written wrapper.
MCP changes that by giving every tool the same shape, so one adapter can understand all of them at once.

items: No more writing a new LangChain Tool subclass for every external service.
Any MCP server, written by anyone, becomes usable the moment you connect to it.
The tool ecosystem grows for every LangChain user at the same time it grows for every other MCP client.

blocks.text: 2. What langchain-mcp-adapters Actually Does
The package sits between an MCP client connection and LangChain's own Tool abstraction.
It reads the list of tools an MCP server exposes and converts each entry into a LangChain StructuredTool automatically.
No manual schema translation is needed, the adapter handles input schemas, descriptions, and the actual invocation call.

blocks.title: One adapter, any server
blocks.content: The adapter does not care what a specific MCP server does. It only needs the server to speak the MCP protocol correctly, and the tools show up ready to use.

blocks.text: 3. Installing the Package
The adapter is a small Python package that depends on both the mcp package and core LangChain pieces.

code.content: pip install langchain-mcp-adapters langchain langgraph mcp

blocks.text: Everything here is async under the hood, since MCP communication itself is async, so your code needs an event loop running.
4. Connecting to an MCP Server from LangChain
Before you can load any tools, you need a live MCP client session, exactly like any other MCP client would open.

code.content:
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

server_params = StdioServerParameters(
    command="python",
    args=["weather_server.py"],
)

async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
    async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
        await session.initialize()
        # session is now ready for the adapter to use

blocks.text: That initialize call is the same handshake every MCP client performs, nothing about it is specific to LangChain.
5. Loading Tools with load_mcp_tools

blocks.alt: A call to load mcp tools converts server tools into LangChain tools

blocks.text: Once a session is open, a single function call turns the server's entire tool list into LangChain tools.

code.content:
from langchain_mcp_adapters.tools import load_mcp_tools

async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
    async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
        await session.initialize()
        tools = await load_mcp_tools(session)
        print([t.name for t in tools])

blocks.text: The returned list is a plain list of LangChain Tool objects, ready to hand to any agent that expects tools.

7. Wiring Tools into an Agent Executor

blocks.alt: Loaded tools are wired into an agent executor before it can use them

blocks.text: With a tool list in hand, building an agent is exactly the same as building one with any hand written tool.

code.content:
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic

model = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-5")
agent = create_react_agent(model, tools)

result = await agent.ainvoke({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Paris?"}]
})

blocks.text: The agent has no idea these tools came from an MCP server, it just sees ordinary LangChain tools it can call.
8. MultiServerMCPClient for Several Servers at Once

blocks.alt: One client connects to several MCP servers at once

blocks.text: Real agents usually need more than one tool source, so the package ships a client that manages several servers together.

code.content:
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient

client = MultiServerMCPClient({
    "filesystem": {"command": "python", "args": ["fs_server.py"], "transport": "stdio"},
    "github": {"url": "https://mcp.example.com/github", "transport": "streamable_http"},
})

tools = await client.get_tools()
agent = create_react_agent(model, tools)

blocks.text: The agent still just sees one flat tool list, it never needs to know which server any single tool actually came from.
9. Async Nature of MCP Tools in LangChain
Every MCP tool call travels over a network or subprocess boundary, so the adapted tools are async by nature.
Calling them from synchronous code still works, LangChain wraps the async call for you, but it is slower than calling them natively with await.

blocks.title: Prefer ainvoke over invoke
blocks.content: When your tools come from MCP, use the async agent methods, ainvoke and astream, rather than their sync counterparts, to avoid unnecessary blocking.

blocks.text: 10. Structured Output and Content Blocks
An MCP tool can return more than plain text, it can return images or other structured content blocks.
The adapter flattens these content blocks into the format a LangChain ToolMessage expects, so the agent still sees a normal message.
If a tool returns an image block, that image travels through as part of the tool message content, the same as any multimodal LangChain tool.
11. Handling Errors from MCP Tools inside an Agent

blocks.alt: An MCP tool error inside an agent is caught rather than crashing the run

blocks.text: An MCP tool can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with LangChain, a bad argument, a downstream API outage, a timeout.
Individual tool call failures show up to the agent as a normal tool error message, which the model can read and react to.
12. Session Management and Client Lifecycles
An MCP session needs to stay open for as long as the agent might call its tools, closing it early breaks every tool that came from it.
Most real applications open the session once at startup, build the agent, and only close the session when the app shuts down.
MultiServerMCPClient takes care of this for multiple servers, so you rarely need to manage raw sessions by hand once you use it.

blocks.text: 14. Where This Fits in LangGraph
LangGraph is LangChain's newer graph based agent runtime, and MCP adapted tools plug into it exactly the same way.
A tool node in a LangGraph graph can hold a mix of hand written tools and MCP adapted tools with no special casing needed.
This matters because it means MCP does not lock you into one particular agent framework or style of building agents.
15. Security and Trust Considerations

blocks.alt: A trusted MCP server is compared against an unvetted one when wired into an agent

blocks.text: An MCP adapted tool still runs with whatever permissions the underlying MCP server has, the adapter adds no extra sandboxing.
Connecting an agent to an untrusted MCP server means trusting that server with anything the agent decides to send it.

items: Only connect to MCP servers you trust or have reviewed.
Review tool descriptions before handing them to a model, since the model reads them as instructions too.
Scope database or filesystem access on the server side, not just on the agent side.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Here is a small but complete agent that pulls tools from two MCP servers and answers a question using both.

code.content:
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic

client = MultiServerMCPClient({
    "notes": {"command": "python", "args": ["notes_server.py"], "transport": "stdio"},
    "weather": {"url": "https://mcp.example.com/weather", "transport": "streamable_http"},
})

tools = await client.get_tools()
model = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-5")
agent = create_react_agent(model, tools)

response = await agent.ainvoke({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Check my notes for the trip city, then get the weather there."}]
})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)

blocks.text: Neither server needed to know anything about LangChain, and the agent never needed a single hand written tool wrapper.
Adding a third server later takes the same one line change, no rewrite of the agent logic itself.
Common Mistakes

items: Closing the MCP session before the agent finishes using its tools, which breaks every call that follows.
Calling adapted tools with the synchronous agent API and wondering why everything feels slow.
Connecting to an unfamiliar MCP server without reading what its tools actually do first.
Forgetting that MultiServerMCPClient merges tool names, so two servers with clashing tool names can collide.
Assuming load_mcp_tools refreshes automatically if the server's tool list changes, it does not, you need to reload it.
Skipping error handling around tool loading, so one unreachable server crashes the whole agent startup.

blocks.text: Practice
Take any MCP server you already built in an earlier lesson and connect it to a LangChain agent using load_mcp_tools.

code.content:
tools = await load_mcp_tools(session)
agent = create_react_agent(model, tools)
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "List what tools you have."}]})

blocks.text: Then add a second MCP server with MultiServerMCPClient and confirm the agent can use tools from both in one conversation.
Finally, try renaming one tool on the server side and check that the agent picks up the change after a reload.
Key Takeaway
langchain-mcp-adapters turns any MCP server's tools into ordinary LangChain tools automatically, no custom wrapper code required.
That means a LangChain agent can reuse the entire, growing MCP tool ecosystem instead of every integration being written from scratch.
